5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
The last chapter moves from prophetic warning to pastoral tenderness. It opens with the letter’s most severe passage (vv. 1–6), a woe against rich oppressors who withheld wages and lived in luxury while the righteous suffered. Their judgment is certain.

Then James turns gently to the suffering church (vv. 7–20). Be patient like a farmer waiting for the rains, because the Lord is coming and the Judge is at the door. Do not grumble or swear. Pray in every condition: in suffering, in gladness, in sickness, confessing sins to one another. Elijah was a man like us, and his prayers were heard. And the letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James addresses the rich oppressors as the prophets did. Weep and howl: your wealth has rotted, your clothes are moth-eaten, your gold has rusted, and the rust will testify against you. The wages you withheld from your harvesters cry out, and the Lord of hosts has heard. You have fattened yourselves for a day of slaughter, and condemned the righteous who did not resist.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

Hoarded wealth will testify against those who kept back the wages of their labourers. The cries of the harvesters have reached the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A day-labourer's withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Now: Comfort bought by someone else's hunger is not a blessing but fattening for a day of slaughter.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now listen, you rich people: weep and wail because of the misery coming on you. Your wealth has rotted, moths have eaten your clothes, your gold and silver are corroded, and their corrosion will testify against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have hoarded wealth in the last days.

Prophetic woe. Like Amos, James addresses the oppressors directly while the oppressed listen. Probably not church members.

Three assets fail. Riches rot like grain; fine clothes, a form of savings, are moth-eaten; gold and silver corrode. Gold does not corrode, and James knows it. The overstatement makes the point: even what cannot decay has decayed.

Rust as witness. A legal word. Spent money does not rust. This rusted because it was hoarded while those who earned it went hungry.

The last days. They accumulated in the very time it could least help them, like buying property in a town about to flood.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth is sinful in itself. Abraham and Job were rich. The sin is hoarding and oppression.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields cry out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence, fattening yourselves for the day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the innocent, who were not resisting you.

Withheld wages. The law required day-labourers to be paid before sunset (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). A withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Crying out. Like Abel’s blood (Genesis 4:10). And the title “Lord of hosts”, the LORD of armies, is chosen on purpose: the workers had no court, but their case has been heard by the commander of heaven.

Comfort bought by hunger. Not wealth in the abstract, but luxury at one table funded by hunger at another.

Fattened. The beast grazes happily, not knowing what the day is for.

No resistance. The law was used against those who could not afford it (2:6). There was never a contest.

On a Tuesday. A small business owner pays suppliers and staff on time even when it squeezes him. A shopper asks who made her cheap clothes, and at what wage. James says God hears the cries of the underpaid. So should we.
verseByVerse.note: The Law required day-labourers to be paid the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be patient until the Lord comes, as a farmer waits for the rains. Do not grumble against one another; the Judge is at the door. Remember the prophets and Job, and how compassionate the Lord is. Do not swear; let your yes be yes. Pray in suffering, praise in gladness, and call the elders in sickness. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another. Elijah was a man like us, and his prayers were answered. And if anyone wanders from the truth, go and bring him back.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith

Be patient as the farmer waits for the rains, because the Lord is coming. Pray in every condition; the prayer of faith is prayer submitted to God's will, and Elijah was a man like us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pressed from outside, the congregation was grumbling against one another.

Now: The letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be patient, then, brothers and sisters, until the Lord comes. See how the farmer waits for the land to yield its valuable crop, patiently waiting for the autumn and spring rains. You too be patient and stand firm, because the Lord’s coming is near.

Long-tempered. The word is makrothymia, patience with difficult people, not just endurance. After hearing their oppressors denounced, the temptation is to take matters into their own hands. James says: wait.

Waiting for someone to act. Not because injustice does not matter, but because the Lord of hosts has heard.

The farmer. Autumn rains soften the ground for sowing; spring rains swell the grain. Between them, no activity brings the harvest a day sooner.

Establish your hearts. Prop them up. Waiting needs strengthening.

Was James wrong? “At hand” means Christ’s coming is the next great event in God’s plan and could happen at any time, not that it would come within a few years. Peter answers the same objection: with the Lord a day is as a thousand years, and the delay is patience (2 Peter 3:8–9).
verseByVerse.note: In Israel the early rain came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rain in spring, before harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, or you will be judged. The Judge is standing at the door.

Grumbling. Not open quarrels but muttering: the complaint under the breath.

Pressure goes sideways. Pressure from outside that cannot be released outwards is released onto the people nearest. A church under strain turns on itself, quietly.

At the door. Comfort: the oppressed are told their Judge has arrived. And warning: he is at the door of their room too, about to walk in on the muttering.

On a Tuesday. A stressful week at work, and you come home and snap at your family. Notice where the pressure is going. Take it to God instead, and apologise to them.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the prophets who spoke in the Lord’s name as an example of patience in suffering. We call blessed those who endured. You have heard of Job’s endurance and seen how the Lord finally dealt with him: the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

The prophets. They suffered because of their faithfulness. These believers are in the succession, not the exception.

Job. Not “patient” in the English sense: he protested, demanded a hearing, argued his case. What he did was not let go. Steadfastness has room for a man who complains bitterly and will not walk away.

The end of the story. Job could not see it from inside; the reader can. And James draws a striking conclusion from a book that never explains Job’s suffering: the end showed what God is like, “compassionate and merciful”, echoing God’s own name at Sinai, “merciful and gracious” (Exodus 34:6).

For worship. When you cannot see the purpose of your suffering, remember Job’s ending. The Lord has not stopped being compassionate.

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, do not swear, by heaven or earth or anything else. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, so that you will not be condemned.

Jesus’ words. James echoes his brother almost exactly (Matthew 5:34–37).

Graded oaths. People swore by heaven, earth, the temple or their own head, with some oaths held binding and others understood as escape routes. A man who must swear to be believed admits his ordinary word is unreliable.

Are all oaths forbidden? Quakers and many Anabaptists say yes. But God swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as witness (Romans 1:9), and Jesus answered under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). So the Reformed confessions allow solemn, lawful oaths, in court or in marriage vows. What James forbids is casual swearing and oaths used to make some words binding and others not.

On a Tuesday. Do the people who know you best need you to say “I promise” or “honestly” before they believe you? Let your plain word be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you in trouble? Let him pray. Is anyone happy? Let him sing praise.

Every condition God-ward. Trouble goes up as prayer; joy goes up as song. Between them they cover every day.

The neglected half. Most Christians know trouble should send them to God. Fewer treat gladness the same way. A man who prays only when suffering relates to his own need more than to God.

On a Tuesday. Good news arrives: a job offer, a healthy scan. Before phoning anyone, thank God aloud, or sing.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you sick? Let him call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the Lord’s name. The prayer offered in faith will make the sick person well; the Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.

The sick man calls. And he calls the elders, the ordinary leaders of the local church, not a gifted healer.

Oil. The main verb is pray; anointing is secondary. Oil was both medicine (Luke 10:34) and a sign of setting apart for God; here, with prayer in the Lord’s name, most likely a sign. Churches may still do this. It does not oppose medicine; Christians should use doctors and pray.

Does every prayer of faith heal? No. Asking can be answered no (4:3). Paul’s thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:8–9), and he left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20). “The prayer of faith” is not prayer with enough confidence; that would make faith a work, and blame the sick for their illness, a cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict. It is prayer in submission to God’s will. “Save” and “raise up” reach beyond recovery: every believer will be raised, whether or not this illness ends.

Last rites? Roman Catholic teaching bases the sacrament of anointing of the sick on this verse, once given mainly to the dying. But James speaks of praying for recovery, not preparing for death, and healing comes from the Lord, not from a sacrament.

If he has sinned. Careful and merciful. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it, the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.
verseByVerse.note: Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.

To one another. Not to a priest, and not only to God. Ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves. It needs no office and is almost always avoided.

Why it works. Sin kept private grows in the dark, fed by fear of exposure. Once you have told someone, it has lost its cover. And confession is joined to prayer: you tell someone, and they pray for you.

Healed. The whole person, body and soul. But not every sickness comes from sin: “if he has committed sins” (v. 15), and Jesus denied it of the man born blind (John 9:3).

Righteous. Not a rare spiritual class. The next verse names Elijah, “a man with a nature like ours”.

On a Tuesday. A man has hidden a pornography habit for years. He finally tells a trusted friend, who prays with him and checks in weekly. For the first time, the habit begins to lose its grip.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah was a human being just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years. Then he prayed again, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth produced its crops.

Like us. James says this first. The most spectacular prophet, with fire from heaven, is exactly the one we would say proves prayer works for other people. But right after Carmel he ran into the desert and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4).

Prayed with prayer. A Hebrew idiom for earnest prayer. 1 Kings records Elijah announcing the drought; James understands the announcement to rest on prayer. Jesus gives the same length, three and a half years (Luke 4:25).

Rain again. The picture returns to the farmer waiting for rain (v. 7). The letter ties itself together.

For worship. The God who heard Elijah hears ordinary believers. Pray boldly.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah’s prayers are implied in 1 Kings; Jesus also gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers and sisters, if one of you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, remember this: whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save him from death and cover a multitude of sins.

No farewell. The letter ends without blessing or greeting, on the subject of someone else’s soul.

Wanders. To drift off course: the root of our word “planet”, a wandering star. Nobody announces they are leaving.

Someone. Not the elders, not a teacher. Anyone who notices and goes after him.

Save from death. As high a claim as could be made for ordinary pastoral care. The covering of sins is God’s work (Proverbs 10:12); the one who goes after the wanderer is his means.

Can a true believer be lost? Arminian Christians read the verse that way. The more likely reading is that the wanderer is either a believer whom God restores through others’ loving pursuit, or a professing member whose wandering would show his faith was never real. Either way, the one who brings him back is God’s means of keeping him. That is why we must not leave wanderers alone.

On a Tuesday. Someone has stopped coming to church. Not a dramatic exit; they just drifted. Send the message today. Ask how they are. Offer coffee. James ends his letter with a man walking out to look for somebody.

He does not resist you.<sup>7</sup>Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.<sup>8</sup>You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.<sup>9</sup>Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.<sup>10</sup>As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.<sup>11</sup>Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.<sup>12</sup>But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.<sup>13</sup>Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.<sup>14</sup>Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.<sup>15</sup>And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.<sup>16</sup>Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.<sup>17</sup>Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth.<sup>18</sup>Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.<sup>19</sup>My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back,<sup>20</sup>let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
